text: The Boeing Company, along with its subsidiaries, is one of the world’s major aerospace firms and operates in four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC). The Commercial Airplanes segment develops, produces, and markets commercial jet aircraft to the global airline industry, offering a family of jetliners including the 737 narrow-body and 767, 777, and 787 wide-body models, with production of the 747 ending in 2022. Development continues on the 777X program and the 737-7 and 737-10 derivatives. The Defense, Space & Security segment produces and modifies manned and unmanned military aircraft, weapons systems, and related products such as strategic defense systems, C4ISR, cyber solutions, satellite systems, and space exploration. The Global Services segment provides a full range of services to commercial and defense customers, including supply chain management, engineering, maintenance, upgrades, spare parts, training, technical documentation, and data analytics. Boeing Capital provides financing to customers to purchase and take delivery of Boeing products, managing financing exposure through equipment leases, sales-type/finance leases, notes, receivables, assets held for sale or re-lease, and investments. Boeing owns numerous patents and licenses intellectual property from third parties, including U.S. government licenses for inventions developed under government contracts, and also relies on unpatented research, engineering skills, trademarks, trade secrets, and other intellectual property. As of December 31, 2022, Boeing’s total workforce was approximately 156,000, with 13% located outside the U.S., and included about 50,000 union members. The company has major collective bargaining agreements with the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (20% of employees, expiring in September 2024 and July 2025), the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (10%, expiring in October 2026), and the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (1%, expiring in April 2027). Boeing is committed to diversity and inclusion, with a workforce composition in the U.S. as of December 2021 of approximately 23% women, 33% U.S. racial and ethnic minorities, and 15% U.S. veterans, and supports over 15,000 participants in 170 global Business Resource Groups. In 2022, Boeing hired approximately 23,000 new employees for critical skills, with a 78% offer acceptance rate and a voluntary resignation rate of about 4%. Employees engage in ongoing feedback through surveys from pre-hire to exit, and the company maintains a multi-level recognition program for performance. In 2022, Boeing employees completed approximately 5.8 million hours of learning, with over 9,000 employees annually using tuition assistance to pursue degrees, certificates, or courses from more than 300 accredited institutions worldwide. Safety, quality, integrity, and sustainability are central to Boeing’s operations, with a commitment to zero workplace injuries and an annual Code of Conduct signed by employees to uphold ethical and compliant work practices. Employees can report concerns related to ethics or safety through multiple channels, and the company addresses such concerns to uphold its values. The commercial jet aircraft market is highly competitive, with strong international competitors such as Airbus and emerging players from China, and Boeing focuses on product improvements, cost reduction, and delivering superior design, safety, efficiency, and value. The Defense, Space & Security segment competes with Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon Technologies, General Dynamics, SpaceX, and non-U.S. companies like BAE Systems and Airbus Group, which are expanding their U.S. presence through partnerships. In the commercial and defense services markets, BGS faces similar competition and intends to grow market share through high customer satisfaction and productivity. Boeing’s businesses are heavily regulated, working with U.S. government agencies such as the U.S. military, NASA, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and the Department of Homeland Security, as well as equivalent authorities in non-U.S. markets. Government contracts may be terminated at the government’s convenience or for default; in the case of convenience termination, Boeing is entitled to payment for completed work and allowable termination costs, while in default termination, the government pays only for accepted work and may require Boeing to cover the cost difference to reprocure the items. For default, Boeing may also face liability for damages. Commercial aircraft must comply with FAA regulations on production, quality, airworthiness, repair procedures, and operational safety, with new models requiring FAA certification before service; similar requirements exist outside the U.S. under national aviation authorities, coordinated in Europe by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency. Boeing is subject to environmental laws and regulations regarding the discharge, treatment, storage, disposal, and remediation of hazardous substances and wastes, as well as climate change-related laws affecting greenhouse gas emissions, which could increase compliance costs, energy and raw material expenses, and investment in new technologies. Environmental compliance costs are a normal, recurring part of operations and are often allowable under U.S. government contracts. It is reasonably possible that increased environmental compliance costs could materially impact Boeing’s results of operations, financial condition, or cash flows if stricter clean-up standards or new contamination areas are imposed. For further details on environmental contingencies, see Note 13 to the Consolidated Financial Statements. Non-U.S. sales are subject to both U.S. and non-U.S. governmental regulations and procurement policies, including import-export controls and tariffs.

Boeing’s operations are subject to environmental regulations related to climate change, including laws that limit or govern greenhouse gas emissions. These regulations could increase environmental compliance expenses, raise energy and raw material costs, and require new or additional investments in design and technology. The company continuously evaluates its environmental compliance and management to ensure adherence to all applicable laws and regulations. Investigation, remediation, and ongoing operation and maintenance costs associated with environmental compliance are routine and recurring parts of its operations, and such costs are often allowable under its U.S. government contracts. It is reasonably possible that costs to maintain environmental compliance could materially affect the company’s results of operations, financial condition, or cash flows if regulators impose stricter cleanup standards, new areas of soil, air, or groundwater contamination are discovered, or the scope of required work expands. For further details on environmental contingencies, refer to Note 13 in the Consolidated Financial Statements. Non-U.S. sales are subject to both U.S. and non-U.S. governmental regulations and procurement policies, including import-export controls, tariffs, investment rules, exchange controls, anti-corruption measures, and repatriation of earnings, and are exposed to currency, political, and economic risks. Boeing is highly dependent on the availability of key raw materials, parts, and subassemblies from suppliers and subcontractors, primarily aluminum (sheet, plate, forgings, and extrusions), titanium (sheet, plate, forgings, and extrusions), and composites (including carbon and boron). Although alternative sources exist, qualification can take a year or more. In 2022, due to the Russia-Ukraine war, Boeing suspended purchasing titanium from Russia, which did not disrupt operations because it used inventory on hand and identified alternative sources. Many major components and equipment are procured or subcontracted on a sole-source basis, and the company continues to work with a small number of sole-source suppliers to ensure supply continuity. Boeing relies on a large number of U.S. and non-U.S. suppliers and subcontractors to meet performance specifications, quality standards, and delivery schedules at anticipated costs. While the company maintains an extensive qualification and performance surveillance system to manage third-party risks, supplier or subcontractor failures could negatively affect production schedules and program profitability, jeopardizing customer commitments. The company is also dependent on affordable access to energy sources like electricity. No material portion of Boeing’s business is considered seasonal. A significant portion of Boeing’s revenue comes from commercial airlines, which are subject to market volatility. Demand for commercial aircraft is driven by long-term trends in airline passenger and cargo traffic, influenced by economic growth, political stability, airline profitability, aircraft financing, trade policies, government relations, technological advances, fuel prices, terrorism, pandemics, epidemics, and environmental regulations. The airline industry is cyclical and competitive, with significant profit swings, and deterioration in the global economy or financial instability among major customers could reduce new orders, cause delays or cancellations of contracts, or lead to lower revenues, profitability, and cash flows, especially given that the commercial aircraft backlog spans several years. Boeing enters into firm fixed-price aircraft sales contracts with indexed price escalation clauses, which could result in losses if cost overruns occur or if cost increases exceed the escalation rate. Pricing is based on fixed amounts adjusted by formulas derived from labor, commodity, and other price indices, which are outside the company’s control and can fluctuate significantly, impacting revenue and operating margins. A significant portion of revenues comes from a limited number of commercial airlines, and there is no assurance that customers will exercise purchase options, fulfill commitments, or buy additional products or services. Fleet decisions, airline consolidations, or financial difficulties among major customers could reduce revenues and limit profit opportunities. Airlines are facing rising fuel and other costs, and the global economy is experiencing high inflation. Boeing’s Commercial Airplanes business depends on maintaining a healthy production system, ensuring every aircraft meets exacting specifications, achieving production targets, successfully developing and certifying new or derivative aircraft, and meeting stringent performance and reliability standards. The business is highly complex, involving extensive coordination with U.S. and non-U.S. suppliers, skilled labor, and evolving regulatory requirements. The FAA has implemented safety reforms, including the 2018 FAA Reauthorization Act and the 2020 Aircraft Certification, Safety and Accountability Act (ACSAA). Section 116 of ACSAA prohibited the FAA from issuing a type certificate to aircraft after December 27, 2022, unless the aircraft’s flight crew alerting system met certain specifications. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 amended Section 116, so applications for original or amended type certifications submitted before December 27, 2020—including those for the 737-7 and 737-10—are no longer subject to the crew alerting requirements. Beginning one year after the FAA issues a type certificate for the 737-10, any new 737 MAX aircraft must include certain safety enhancements to receive an original airworthiness certification, which are included in Boeing’s 737-10 certification application and will be evaluated by the FAA. Beginning three years after the issuance of a type certificate for the 737-10, all previously delivered 737 MAX aircraft must be retrofitted with these safety enhancements, and as the holder of the type certificate, Boeing is responsible for any associated retrofit costs. The company has provisioned for these estimated costs and does not expect them to be material. Delays in certification or incorporating safety enhancements could negatively impact future revenues, cash flows, and results of operations. Comparable agencies in other countries may adopt similar regulations, and if the FAA or similar foreign agencies implement more stringent rules, Boeing may incur additional compliance costs. The introduction of new programs or derivatives, such as the 777X, 737-7, and 737-10, involves increased risks related to meeting development, testing, certification, and production schedules. Boeing has experienced production quality issues, including in the supply chain, which contributed to reduced 787 deliveries, including a suspension from May 2021 to August 2022. The company continues inspections and rework on stored 787 aircraft. Some customers have contractual rights to compensation for late deliveries or to reject individual aircraft. Delays on the 737, 777X, and 787 programs have led to, and may continue to lead to, customer rights to terminate orders, receive compensation, or substitute orders with other Boeing aircraft. Boeing must minimize production disruptions, achieve operational stability, and implement productivity improvements to meet customer demand and maintain profitability. The company has announced plans to adjust production rates on several programs. The 787 program is currently producing at low rates and is expected to gradually increase to 5 per month in 2023. 777X production is currently paused and expected to resume in 2023. The 737 program has stabilized at 31 per month due to operational and supply chain challenges, with plans to gradually increase production based on market demand and supply chain capacity. If production changes at any commercial aircraft assembly facility are delayed or cause significant disruption, or if suppliers fail to deliver components at required cost and rates, Boeing may be unable to meet delivery schedules or achieve financial performance targets. Operational challenges, such as supplier delays, internal performance failures, or regulatory approval delays, could result in out-of-sequence work, increased production costs, delayed deliveries, impacts to aircraft performance, and higher warranty or fleet support costs. Boeing and its suppliers are experiencing supply chain disruptions due to the lingering effects of COVID-19, global supply chain constraints, and labor instability, along with inflationary pressures. These factors have reduced productivity and negatively affected financial position, results of operations, and cash flows. If Boeing’s commercial aircraft fail to meet performance or reliability requirements or required sustainability standards, the company could face additional costs or lower revenues. Developing and manufacturing aircraft to meet performance, reliability, and sustainability standards is costly and technologically challenging, especially for newer programs. Any failure of a Boeing aircraft to meet these standards could disrupt operations, increase costs, and reduce revenues. Changes in U.S. government defense spending or acquisition priorities could negatively impact financial results. A substantial portion of Boeing’s revenue comes from the U.S. government, primarily from defense programs with the U.S. Department of Defense (U.S. DoD). U.S. defense spending is difficult to predict and may be affected by the national security threat environment, national security strategy, foreign policy, domestic politics, macroeconomic conditions, and legislative actions such as authorization and appropriations bills. The timeliness of FY24 and future appropriations remains a recurring risk; a lapse in funding could cause a government shutdown, impacting operations, while Continuing Resolutions would restrict program activities and delay new programs. Long-term uncertainty persists regarding overall defense spending in FY24 and beyond, with U.S. discretionary spending, including defense, likely to face continued pressure. There remains uncertainty about future acquisition priorities and program-level appropriations, including shifts in national security and defense priorities, and tensions between modernization, sustainment, and investment in new technologies. Changes in investment priorities or budget cuts, including those from the authorizations and appropriations process, could result in reductions, cancellations, or delays of existing or future contracts or programs, materially affecting financial results. Due to ongoing uncertainty about U.S. defense spending and the evolving threat environment, the U.S. DoD is expected to emphasize affordability, innovation, cybersecurity, and delivery of technical data and software in procurement, including implementing cybersecurity compliance requirements for the Defense Industrial Base, which the supply chain may not yet be fully prepared for. Boeing and its suppliers must successfully adapt to these changing priorities or face adverse impacts on revenues and market share. The company’s ability to deliver products and services that meet customer requirements depends heavily on the performance and financial stability of its subcontractors and suppliers, as well as on the availability of skilled labor, raw materials, and components. Boeing relies on other companies, including U.S. and non-U.S. suppliers and subcontractors, to provide raw materials, integrated components, sub-assemblies, and services. Many suppliers are experiencing inflation and disruptions due to the lingering effects of COVID-19, global supply chain constraints, and labor instability. If one or more suppliers or subcontractors face financial difficulties, delivery delays, or performance issues, Boeing may be unable to meet customer commitments, negatively impacting its financial position, results of operations, and cash flows. If key raw materials such as aluminum, titanium, or composites become unavailable or are available only at very high prices, Boeing may be unable to deliver products on time or at budgeted costs. For example, in 2022, Boeing suspended purchasing titanium from Russia due to the Russia-Ukraine war. The company believes it has sufficient materials and parts to avoid near-term production disruptions, but future supply chain impacts remain possible. In some cases, Boeing depends on a single source of supply. A service disruption from such a supplier—due to geopolitical developments or performance or financial issues—could have a material adverse effect on the company’s ability to meet customer commitments or increase operating costs. Competition in the markets in which Boeing operates may reduce future contracts and sales. Competition in its markets is intense, with some competitors having more advanced engineering, manufacturing, or marketing capabilities. In the BCA business, Boeing faces aggressive international competition seeking to gain market share, while in the BDS business, defense industry consolidation, shifting government acquisition priorities, and cost pressures from U.S. and non-U.S. defense customers are intensifying competition. The BGS segment also faces competition from similar U.S. and non-U.S. companies. Increased international competition, cross-border consolidations, and U.S. procurement and compliance requirements may limit Boeing’s cost competitiveness abroad. There is no guarantee Boeing will successfully compete, and such pressures could reduce revenues and market share. A significant portion of Boeing’s revenues comes from non-U.S. sales; in 2022, non-U.S. customers—including foreign military sales (FMS)—accounted for about 41% of revenues, and this share is expected to remain substantial. Doing business internationally exposes Boeing to risks such as changes in regulatory requirements, executive orders, global trade disputes, sourcing restrictions, local funding requirements, currency fluctuations, political and economic volatility, the need for non-U.S. representatives, financing uncertainties, funding credit or guarantee limitations, taxes, export controls, tariffs, embargoes, sanctions (such as those on Russia), trade restrictions, operational complexity, compliance with local and U.S. laws, and unforeseen events like terrorism, war, epidemics, or international conflicts. Since 2018, the U.S. and China have imposed tariffs on each other’s imports, affecting certain aircraft parts Boeing procures; Boeing mitigates these costs through Duty Drawback Customs procedures. The U.S.-China trade relationship remains stalled due to economic and national security concerns. China is a key market for commercial aircraft, and Boeing has long-standing relationships with Chinese customers who are a major part of its commercial aircraft backlog. However, the resumption of 737 MAX deliveries in China is still pending final regulatory approvals, and failure to secure new orders from China could harm market share. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Boeing suspended operations in Russia due to sanctions and export controls, and the war has negatively impacted, and may continue to adversely impact, Boeing’s business and financial results. Deterioration in trade relations between the U.S. and other countries could materially harm Boeing’s financial position, results of operations, and cash flows. Boeing makes estimates and assumptions in accounting for contracts and programs, which involve judgment in assessing risks, estimating revenues and costs, and forecasting schedules and technical performance. Due to the size and complexity of many contracts, estimating total revenues and costs at completion is difficult and subject to many variables, including wage and benefit increases, material prices, fixed costs, and inflation indices. Incentives and penalties are considered when estimating sales and profit rates and are recorded when sufficient information is available to assess performance. Customer and supplier claims are also evaluated. For commercial aircraft programs, inventoriable production costs, tooling, and warranty costs are accumulated and charged to cost of sales by program rather than by individual units. A program is defined by an estimated number of units to be produced over a long-term effort, based on firm orders, letters of intent, and market studies. Changes in customer mix, production costs, learning curves, price escalations, derivative aircraft costs, supplier performance, negotiations, or certification issues can affect these estimates. For development programs like the 777X, 737-7, and 737-10, risks related to certification timing and conditions—such as delays or changes in certification processes—could impact program status. Any change in these estimates could adversely affect future financial performance. Because of the significant judgment involved, materially different revenues and profits could result from different assumptions, revised estimates, or changes in circumstances. Changes in assumptions or conditions could negatively affect future financial results. Boeing may not realize the anticipated benefits of mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures, or divestitures. Success depends on the ability to integrate acquired operations, the performance of the product and service portfolio, and the management team. Financial results could be harmed by unanticipated performance issues, legacy liabilities, transaction-related charges, amortization of intangible assets, asset impairments, credit guarantees, partner performance, or indemnifications. Consolidations of joint ventures could also affect reported results. While Boeing has established procedures to mitigate these risks, there is no assurance of success. Divestitures may result in continued financial involvement through guarantees or other arrangements, and nonperformance by divested businesses could lead to additional payments, higher costs, or asset write-downs. A significant portion of Boeing’s business is conducted under U.S. government contracts, which are subject to unique risks. In 2022, 40% of Boeing’s revenues came from U.S. government contracts, including FMS. These contracts are subject to extensive procurement regulations, and changes to these regulations could increase compliance costs or reduce operating margins. New regulations, climate or cyber-related disclosures, or changes to existing requirements could increase costs or lead to withheld payments or reduced future business. Proposals to raise domestic content thresholds could negatively impact Boeing’s business. U.S. government contracts may be modified, curtailed, or terminated without notice, either at the government’s convenience or for performance defaults. Funding may be reduced or withheld due to fiscal constraints, shifts in national security priorities, or through temporary funding measures like continuing resolutions. Any loss of expected funding or termination of major programs could materially harm financial results. Boeing is subject to U.S. government audits and investigations, including reviews by the Defense Contract Audit Agency and Defense Contract Management Agency, which assess cost structures, compliance with laws, and internal controls. Misclassified or inaccurately allocated costs are deemed non-reimbursable, and previously reimbursed amounts must be refunded. Inadequacies in systems or policies could result in withheld payments, penalties, or reduced future business. If an audit uncovers improper or illegal activities, Boeing could face civil or criminal penalties, contract termination, forfeiture of profits, fines, or debarment from U.S. government contracts. Reputational harm could occur even if allegations are later found false. Boeing enters into fixed-price contracts, which expose it to losses if actual costs exceed estimated revenues. In 2022, approximately 60% of BDS and 69% of BGS revenues came from fixed-price contracts. While these contracts allow for cost reductions and efficiency gains, they also carry the risk of reduced margins or losses if cost overruns occur. If estimated costs exceed estimated prices, Boeing recognizes reach-forward losses, which can significantly affect reported results. For example, in 2022, BDS recorded additional losses on several fixed-price development programs. Near-term production disruptions due to supplier issues, labor instability, and factory performance have led to significant earnings charges, expected to adversely affect future cash flows and potentially result in further charges. New programs also carry risks of reach-forward losses upon award or during performance. Estimating costs for development contracts is more uncertain than for production contracts due to complex designs and technical or quality issues that can cause delays and higher costs, leading to material charges. Key fixed-price development programs include Commercial Crew, KC-46A Tanker, MQ-25, T-7A Red Hawk, VC-25B Presidential Aircraft, and commercial and military satellites. Boeing also enters into cost-type contracts, which account for approximately 40% of BDS and 31% of BGS revenues in 2022. These often involve complex technical challenges and may have uncertain award or incentive fees earned over long periods. Financial risks include reduced fees, lower profit rates, or program cancellation due to cost, schedule, or technical performance issues. Programs such as Ground-based Midcourse Defense, Proprietary, and Space Launch System are primarily cost-type. Some contracts in the commercial satellite and government satellite industries include in-orbit incentive payments, which are paid over time or in full before final acceptance. These payments are at risk if the satellite fails to meet performance specifications for up to 15 years after acceptance. The net present value of expected in-orbit incentive fees is recognized as revenue during construction. If the satellite fails to meet performance criteria, customers may not make future payments, and Boeing may be required to refund amounts or incur significant charges. Unauthorized access to Boeing’s, its customers’, or suppliers’ information systems poses a significant risk. Boeing relies heavily on IT systems and networks, and as cyber threats grow in volume and sophistication, the risk to data confidentiality, integrity, and availability continues to evolve. A cyberattack—whether direct or through the supply chain—could result in loss of intellectual property, unauthorized access to sensitive data, operational disruption, or compromised products. Boeing maintains technical security controls, policy enforcement, monitoring systems, and a Cybersecurity Governance Council to manage these risks. In November 2022, Boeing discovered a cybersecurity incident affecting Jeppesen, a wholly owned subsidiary providing flight planning and navigation services. The incident posed no risk to flight safety and was promptly reported to law enforcement, regulators, and customers. An investigation was launched, and additional protective measures were taken. While this incident had no material impact, future incidents could have significant effects on operations and reputation. Boeing also manages information systems for customers and suppliers, many of whom face similar threats. If Boeing fails to protect their confidential, classified, or personally identifiable data, it could suffer reputational damage or financial losses. Business disruptions from threats to physical security, extreme weather, climate change, natural disasters, pandemics, or public health crises could seriously affect future sales, financial condition, or increase costs and expenses. Such disruptions could impact internal operations or those of suppliers, delaying product and service deliveries to customers. Any significant production delays or damage, manipulation, or improper use of Boeing’s or its suppliers’ data and information systems could have serious consequences.

Changes in these assumptions could significantly alter future contributions and annual costs, impacting shareholders’ equity. For U.S. government contracts, pension costs are allocated based on U.S. Cost Accounting Standards, which can affect contract profitability. We also provide health care benefits to retirees and qualifying dependents, with future costs dependent on medical cost estimates. These estimates are subject to change and affect financial statements. The audit also included an unqualified opinion on internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2022. Critical audit matters included cost estimates for fixed-price development contracts such as KC-46A Tanker, Commercial Crew, VC-25B Presidential Aircraft, T-7A Redhawk, and MQ-25, which involved estimating future costs and margins with significant variability due to supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, and inflation, requiring extensive audit effort and specialized judgment. The audit procedures included evaluating management’s methods, assumptions, and ranges of outcomes, inquiring of project managers and engineers, observing project sites, testing data accuracy, and performing retrospective reviews. Another critical audit matter was program accounting estimates for the 777X program, involving estimating sales and costs for the initial program quantity and unsold units, with uncertainty due to market demand and certification challenges, including potential delays and increased costs. Audit procedures included inquiring of sales and pricing personnel, comparing management’s demand estimates to external sources, evaluating historical performance, and assessing assumptions and internal controls. A third critical audit matter was program accounting revenue estimates for the 787 program, where production quality issues and supply chain disruptions increased risk to forecasted revenue due to difficulty in assessing customer consideration for delivery delays.

Production quality issues and supply chain disruptions in the 787 program have increased the risk associated with forecasted revenue estimates, primarily due to difficulties in assessing the value of consideration expected to be provided to customers as a result of delivery delays. The Company uses program accounting to calculate cost of sales and margins for each commercial airplane sold, which requires estimating the revenue expected to be earned upon delivery of aircraft included in the program’s accounting quantity. Although the 787 program resumed deliveries in 2022, the forecasted delivery schedule and the value of consideration for delivery delays remain key factors affecting estimated revenue. Estimation uncertainty arises for aircraft that have reached or are expected to reach a delivery delay period, which grants customers a contractual termination right, and changes to the delivery schedule could result in additional consideration to customers, potentially leading to lower margins or material reach-forward losses. Auditing the estimated revenues for the 787 program involved extensive audit effort, a high degree of auditor judgment, and required professionals with specialized industry experience. The audit procedures included inquiring of management, including operational and supply chain leadership, about assumptions related to supply chain disruption impacts on the delivery schedule and rework completion timelines; evaluating the appropriateness and consistency of management’s methods for developing delivery schedule assumptions, including the impact of production quality issues and supply chain disruptions; inquiring of sales and pricing personnel about the status of current customer contracts and estimated customer consideration; evaluating the consistency of management’s methods and the appropriateness of significant assumptions used in developing revenue estimates for aircraft with or expected to have delivery delays; and testing the effectiveness of internal controls over the review of significant judgments, assumptions, key data, and mathematical extrapolation used in developing key estimates. The Boeing Company Executive Supplemental Savings Plan, as amended and restated on December 21, 2022 and effective January 1, 2022, consists of four components: (i) Extra Deferrals, allowing eligible employees to defer payments of their base salaries and eligible incentive compensation awards; (ii) the Restoration Benefit, designed to restore qualified plan benefits from The Boeing Company 401(k) Retirement Plan (formerly known as the Voluntary Investment Plan) to the extent such benefits are limited by Code sections 415 and 401(a)(17); (iii) Executive Benefit, which includes Company Non-Elective Contributions, DC SERP Contributions, and historic Executive SSP+ Company Contributions; and (iv) DCP Accounts, established for participants in the Deferred Compensation Plan for Employees of The Boeing Company, which was frozen as of December 31, 2018 and merged into this Plan effective January 1, 2022. The Plan was originally established on January 1, 1978, and has been amended and restated over time, including on January 1, 2008 to comply with Code section 409A. As of January 1, 2022, the Plan was amended and restated to (A) reflect the merger of the Deferred Compensation Plan with the Plan, (B) eliminate Restoration SSP+ Company Contributions and Executive SSP+ Company Contributions, (C) add new Restoration True-Up Contributions, Incentive Matching Contributions, and Company Non-Elective Contributions, (D) simplify mid-year enrollment provisions in the Participant Deferral component, and (E) make other changes. The Plan is a nonqualified deferred compensation plan subject to Code section 409A and is intended to be, in part, an excess benefit plan under ERISA section 3(36) to the extent benefits exceed Code section 415 limits; if not an excess benefit plan, it is intended to be an unfunded plan providing deferred compensation to a select group of management or highly compensated employees under ERISA sections 201(2), 301(a)(3), and 401(a)(1). An Employee is eligible to receive DC SERP Contributions for a Plan Year as long as they satisfy either (i) or (ii): (i) hired on or after January 1, 2009, but before January 1, 2020; on the US Executive Payroll in level EL or EV (level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) as of December 31, 2019; not an elected officer; and ineligible to accrue benefits under any defined benefit plan maintained by the Controlled Group; or (ii) hired before January 1, 2009; on the US Executive Payroll (in any level E-1 through E-5) as of December 31, 2019; and not an elected officer. A Participant hired before January 1, 2009 will receive a DC SERP contribution equal to a Contribution Credit times the sum of Base Pay and Cash Incentive for each applicable pay period, with Base Pay and Cash Incentive counted only if (1) the Participant is on the US Executive Payroll during the applicable pay period or (2) the Cash Incentive is paid after termination of employment from the Controlled Group but on or before the Participant receives their final regular paycheck. The Contribution Credit equals 5%, plus, if applicable, 0.5% times the Participant’s whole years of Benefit Service (as defined under the PVP and/or BSS Plan, as applicable, and determined as of January 1, 2016), subject to a limitation, with the supplemental percentage credited for a period not to exceed seven years. This seven-year period begins on January 1, 2016 (or January 1 of the year the Participant attains age 55, or the date of promotion to the US Executive Payroll, whichever is latest) and is measured cumulatively over the Participant’s lifetime. A one-time contribution is available to an Employee who satisfies the requirements in Section 4.5(A)(i) (hired between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2019) and is first promoted to a level of EL or EV (from a position at level ED) during the Plan Year (prior to August 15, 2022, first promoted to a level of E-1 through E-3 from a position at level E-4 or E-5 during the Plan Year). The one-time contribution equals 2% times the sum of (1) the Participant’s Base Pay Rate immediately following the promotion and (2) the Cash Incentive target percentage multiplied by the Base Pay Rate, both as in effect immediately following the promotion, multiplied by the Participant’s whole years of Service as of the date of first promotion to a level of EL or EV (from a position at level ED) (prior to August 15, 2022, to a level of E-1 through E-3 from a position at level E-4 or E-5), with years of Service limited to service earned since the most recent hire date. This amount is credited to the Participant’s Account as of the date of first promotion to a level of EL or EV (referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022), or as soon thereafter as administratively feasible. A Participant who has received a one-time contribution under this Section upon promotion to a level of EL or EV (referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) will be ineligible for any further contributions under this subsection (C)(ii). Article V outlines vesting and forfeiture rules applicable to certain benefits under the Plan. A Participant’s interest in their Extra Deferral Account will be 100% vested at all times. A Participant’s interest in their Restoration Account will be 100% vested at all times. A Participant’s interest in their Executive Benefit Account will be 100% vested at all times, subject to Section 5.5 and Section 5.6. A Participant may forfeit any part or all of their legacy Executive SSP+ Company Contribution Account attributable to Executive SSP+ Company Contributions made on and after January 1, 2017, if any of the following occur while employed by the Controlled Group or within five years after termination: (A) conviction of a felony involving theft, fraud, embezzlement, or other similar unlawful acts against the Controlled Group or its interests, including acts detrimental to or in conflict with the Controlled Group’s interests as determined by the Administrator in its sole discretion; (B) engaging in any activity, whether individually or as an employee, consultant, or otherwise, that the Administrator determines in its sole discretion constitutes competition with any significant aspect of the Controlled Group’s business, including representing, providing services to, or being an employee of or associated in a business capacity with any person or entity in competition with the Controlled Group’s business or taking a position adverse to it, in a manner detrimental, prejudicial, or in conflict with the Controlled Group’s interests; If a Participant has already received or commenced payment of such portion of their Executive SSP+ Company Contribution Account, the Administrator may pursue legal and equitable relief to enforce forfeiture and recover the amount distributed. For DC SERP vesting, no payments shall be made from a Participant’s DC SERP Account except to the extent the Participant is vested. A Participant hired between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2019 will vest 100% in their DC SERP Account component(s) covered under subsection (A) on the date they satisfy any of the following: (i) being on the US Executive Payroll at a level of EL or EV (referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) for 36 consecutive months, with prior periods of employment on the US Executive Payroll at a level of E-1 through E-3 being counted; (ii) dying while an Employee; or (iii) being laid off from a position at level EL or EV (referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) and being eligible for benefits under The Boeing Company Executive Layoff Benefits Plan. Special vesting rules apply to a Participant hired between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2019 who has attained either (i) age 55 with 10 years of Service or (ii) age 62 with one year of Service while employed by the Controlled Group. For a Participant transferring employment directly from the Controlled Group to ULA or USA, uninterrupted service at ULA or USA as an executive in a position at a comparable level will be credited toward the 36 consecutive months requirement, provided the transfer is from the US Executive Payroll (or a position at level EL or EV, if applicable) at the Controlled Group to comparable executive status at ULA or USA. For purposes of computing vesting, a Participant who transfers directly from the Controlled Group to ULA or USA will have uninterrupted service at ULA or USA as an executive in a comparable position credited toward the 36 consecutive months requirement, provided the transfer is from the US Executive Payroll (or a position at level EL or EV, referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) to comparable executive status at ULA or USA. Service at ULA or USA will not be credited for any period prior to the Participant’s attainment of executive status at ULA or USA. If a Participant Separates from Service (other than due to an Authorized Period of Absence) or transfers off the US Executive Payroll (or a position at level EL or EV, referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) before becoming 100% vested in the payroll contribution portion of their DC SERP Account, they will forfeit all rights to the nonvested portion of the account attributable to the period prior to Separation from Service or transfer. Any benefit that becomes vested during an Authorized Period of Absence that continues after a deemed Separation from Service remains subject to the payment timing rules under Section 6.1. If a Participant stops accruing service toward vesting requirements after becoming partially vested in the one-time contribution portion of the DC SERP Account and later resumes accruing service, the accrued amounts after resumption will not be vested until the Participant satisfies the vesting requirements under subsection (A) or (C) following resumption. Separate vesting requirements apply to each component of a Participant’s DC SERP Account described in Sections 4.4(C)(i)(a), (i)(b), and (ii). A Participant who has accrued more than one component (e.g., due to Separation from Service and subsequent rehire) must satisfy the vesting requirements for each component. If a Participant Separates from Service after becoming 100% vested in a particular DC SERP Account component, they will be fully vested in any additional accruals under the same component following rehire or return, even if they fail to meet the 36 consecutive months requirement after rehire or return. However, they will not be fully vested in amounts accrued under a different component unless the corresponding vesting requirements are satisfied. The Administrator may determine, in its sole discretion, that a Participant forfeits any part or all of their DC SERP Account if: (A) the Participant is convicted of a felony involving theft, fraud, embezzlement, or other similar unlawful acts against the Controlled Group or its interests, including acts detrimental to, prejudicial to, or in conflict with the Controlled Group’s interests as determined by the Administrator; (B) the Participant engages in any activity, directly or indirectly, that the Administrator determines constitutes competition with any significant aspect of Controlled Group business, such as representing, providing services to, or being employed by or associated with a business in competition with the Controlled Group or taking a position adverse to the Controlled Group’s business; (C) the Participant, without advance approval from The Boeing Company’s Senior Vice President of Human Resources (or equivalent), induces or attempts to induce any Controlled Group employee, representative, or consultant to terminate or breach their contract with the Controlled Group to work for the Participant or a third party; (D) the Participant disparages the Controlled Group, its products, or its employees in a manner viewed as negative or critical, except for legally protected communications to government agencies or statements made in sworn testimony in administrative, judicial, or arbitral proceedings; or (E) the Participant uses or discloses proprietary or confidential information, including trade secrets, of the Controlled Group after January 1, 2017, except for legally protected communications to government agencies or statements made in sworn testimony. If a Participant has already received or commenced payment of their DC SERP Account, the Administrator may pursue legal or equitable relief to enforce forfeiture and recover the benefit. These forfeiture provisions continue in effect unless modified by a court of competent jurisdiction, and if any portion is held unenforceable, the provisions are deemed amended to the broadest enforceable scope and continue in effect. Additionally, the Administrator may require forfeiture or reimbursement of any portion of a DC SERP Account attributable to an incentive award if the Controlled Group seeks recovery under a clawback provision of a Cash Incentive plan. A Participant may elect the form and timing of distribution for their Extra Deferral Account, with the election required at the time of the first Extra Deferral Election. If a timely election is not made regarding timing, the Participant is deemed to have elected to receive payment in January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service (subject to subsection (H)), and if no timely election is made regarding form, the Participant is deemed to have elected a lump sum. A Participant may change a distribution election (or deemed election) for the entire Extra Deferral Account after the initial election, subject to conditions in subsection (F). For the Restoration Account, a distribution election must be made at the time of the first Restoration Deferral Election or during the enrollment period immediately preceding the first year with a Company contribution, and applies to the entire account, including prior Restoration True-Up Contributions and Restoration SSP+ Company Contributions. If a timely election is not made regarding timing, the Participant is deemed to have elected to receive payment in January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service (subject to subsection (H)), and if no timely election is made regarding form, the Participant is deemed to have elected a lump sum. A Participant may change a distribution election for the entire Restoration Account after the initial election, subject to conditions in subsection (F). For the Executive Benefit Account, no initial distribution election is required; the Participant is deemed to have elected a lump sum payable in January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service (subject to subsection (H)), and may change this deemed election subject to conditions in subsection (F). The lump sum distribution option is a single payment made in the later of: (i) January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service, or (ii) January of the first Plan Year following the Participant’s attainment of a specified age (subject to subsection (E)), as elected by the Participant (subject to subsection (H)). The amount equals the value of the Account as of the first business day of January of the Plan Year of payment (or a specified valuation date), with no additional interest or earnings credited thereafter. The installment payment option involves annual payments for a period between 2 and 15 years, beginning in the later of: (i) January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service, or (ii) January of the first Plan Year following the Participant’s attainment of a specified age (subject to (E)), as elected by the Participant (subject to subsection (H)). Payments continue each January until the full amount is paid. The annual payment amount is calculated by dividing the Account balance as of the first business day of January of the Plan Year of payment (or a specified valuation date) by the number of years remaining in the distribution period, with no additional earnings or interest credited after the valuation date. If a Participant has elected installments and their remaining Account balance is $10,000 or less upon any scheduled payment date (excluding the DCP Account), the entire remaining balance is paid as a final lump sum at that time. A Participant may change a distribution election (or deemed election) for each of the Restoration Account, Executive Benefit Account, Extra Deferral Account, and DCP Account (Deferrals) and DCP Account (Match) only once, provided the new election changes the time of payment (consistent with clause (iii) below) and may change the form of payment (from lump sum to installments or vice versa). Such changes may be made at any time and do not need to occur during an annual enrollment period. If made during the annual enrollment period, the last change on file at the end of the period is irrevocable. If made outside the annual enrollment period or by a Participant who is not an Eligible Employee, the change is irrevocable upon making it. Changes that would defer commencement of any portion of the Restoration Account, Executive Benefit Account, Extra Deferral Account, or DCP Account beyond both age 70½ and Separation from Service are not effective. A new distribution election must be submitted at least 12 months before the existing scheduled distribution date under the applicable subaccount. The revised election must not take effect for at least 12 months after it is made. The new election must provide for an additional deferral period of at least 5 years beyond the original distribution date. Installment payments cannot be changed or revoked once they have begun. All payments are made in January (subject to subsection (H)). Benefits under this Plan begin no later than the first January following the calendar year in which the Participant both attains (or would have attained) age 70½ and is Separated from Service. For Participants actively employed beyond age 70½, benefits begin no later than the first January following the calendar year in which the Participant Separates from Service. Any election to the contrary is not effective. A Specified Employee will not receive any distribution during the six-month period immediately following Separation from Service. The Account of a Specified Employee will be distributed in the form elected (or deemed elected) under subsection (A), (B), or (C), as applicable, and will be made or commence as of the latest of: (1) the time elected (or deemed elected), (2) the month following completion of the six-month waiting period (for Separations from Service between July 1 and December 31), and (3) January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service (for Separations from Service between January 1 and June 30). If a Participant has elected installments, subsequent payments are made in January of each successive year until the Account is exhausted. For Specified Employees who separate from service between July 1 and December 31, distributions will be made in January of the first plan year following separation; for those who separate between January 1 and June 30, distributions will be made in January of the first plan year following separation. If a participant has elected installment payments, subsequent payments will be made in January of each successive year until the account is exhausted. For payments made other than in January, the distribution amount is based on the value of the participant’s account as of the first business day of the month the payment is due (or another valuation date specified by the Administrator), and no additional earnings or interest will be credited to the account after that valuation date. If a Specified Employee dies during the six-month waiting period, the waiting period ends, and benefits will be distributed according to Section 6.2 (Death Benefits). For a participant who is rehired after separation from service or who remains employed during an authorized period of absence or reduced level of services, installment payments that began before rehire (Old Account) will continue without suspension, and the Old Account will be paid until exhausted. If a participant is on an authorized period of absence or reduced level of services and makes deferrals or receives contributions during that time (to the extent vested), those amounts will be distributed in January of the first plan year following the year in which they were made, in accordance with the original distribution election or deemed election. For participants who have not yet begun receiving benefits, the Old Account (to the extent vested) will be distributed in January following the year the participant attains the specified age, regardless of whether a subsequent separation from service occurs after rehire. The New Account will be distributed either in January following the separation from service after rehire or in January following both the separation from service after rehire and attainment of the specified age, as per the original election. Any deferrals or contributions made during an authorized period of absence or reduced level of services (to the extent vested) will be distributed in January following the year the participant attains the specified age, regardless of whether the participant resumes services before benefits begin. The Administrator will establish and maintain an account for each participant for each period of employment, beginning upon eligibility and ending with separation from service. Each account is credited with participant deferrals, company contributions, and earnings credits as described in Section 7.2, and is reduced as payments are made. As part of the January 1, 2019 amendment and restatement of the Plan, certain restoration benefit sub-accounts of participants were transferred from the Plan to The Boeing Company Supplemental Savings Plan (SSP), such that the opening account balances in the SSP on January 1, 2019 equaled the closing balances of the participants’ restoration accounts in the Plan on December 31, 2018. The affected participants were (A) each employee (as defined in the SSP) who was an eligible employee (as defined in the SSP) on January 1, 2019 and was a participant in the restoration benefit of the Plan prior to 2019, and (B) each other current or former employee (as defined in the SSP) who was not as of January 1, 2019 and had never been on the US Executive Payroll (as defined in the Plan). Earnings credits are credited to a participant’s account(s) at the participant’s (or beneficiary’s) election under one or more of the following methods: (i) the Interest Fund method, (ii) the Boeing Stock Fund method, or (iii) the Other Investment Funds method, with the Interest Fund method used if no election is made. Under the Interest Fund method, the sub-account is adjusted daily based on changes in unit value, and interest is calculated each plan year as the mean between the high and low yields on AA-rated industrial bonds as reported by Moody’s Investors Service, Inc. during the first eleven months of the preceding plan year, rounded to the nearest ¼ of one percent, and participants are notified annually of the established rate. Under the Boeing Stock Fund method, the participant’s sub-account is credited with units valued in the same manner as units in the Boeing Stock Fund under the Boeing 401(k), with the number of units recorded for bookkeeping purposes only and not representing actual ownership in Boeing stock or the fund. The number of units is adjusted for stock splits, dividends, and other similar events. Under the Other Investment Funds method, the participant may elect to have their sub-account credited with expenses, income, gains, and losses on investment funds similar to those offered under the Boeing 401(k) (excluding the Boeing Stock Fund and Stable Value Fund), as designated by the Administrator, with the Administrator having the discretion to disregard such elections. Earnings credits may be subject to valuation adjustments as per Administrator-established procedures, but the portion of the account already distributed at the time of the adjustment will not be subject to such adjustment. A participant may change how future additions to their account are invested at any time during the plan year, subject to Administrator rules, and may transfer funds between sub-accounts daily, but not on the same day, and cannot transfer into the Boeing Stock Fund for 30 calendar days after transferring out, regardless of the amount transferred. The participant may continue to direct future additions into the Boeing Stock Fund and make transfers out at any time, subject to insider trading rules. A participant’s account may be forfeited or reduced if the Administrator is unable to locate the participant or beneficiary (a “missing participant”) or if the Administrator recaptures amounts improperly credited to the account. The Plan is administered by the Administrator, who may establish rules, interpretations, determinations, and computations, and any decision by the Administrator regarding eligibility or benefit calculations is conclusive and binding. The Administrator must submit periodic reports to the Compensation Committee. The claims procedure for benefits and appeals is the same as that in the Boeing 401(k), with the Compensation Committee replacing the Administrator for review of claims related to elected officers, except for determinations related to potential forfeiture or reimbursement under Sections 5.5 or 5.7 of the Plan, which are made by the Administrator. The Board of Directors, Compensation Committee, Administrator, and their delegates may amend the Plan at any time, including combining or transferring all or part of the Plan with other plans maintained by the Controlled Group or terminating the Plan for that purpose, but the Compensation Committee has exclusive authority to amend the Plan to change the rate or amount of Company-provided benefits for employees on the US Executive Payroll, and the Board of Directors may terminate the Plan at any time. In the event of amendment or termination, a participant’s benefits will not be less than they would have been if the participant had terminated employment immediately prior to the amendment or termination, adjusted by any earnings credits attributable to periods on or after the effective date. Generally, upon termination of the Plan, participants are not entitled to receive a distribution until the time specified in Article VI. However, The Boeing Company may, in its discretion, terminate the entire Plan and pay each participant a single lump-sum distribution of their entire accrued benefit, subject to conditions under Code section 409A and any IRS or Treasury guidance. Nothing in the Plan grants any right to remain employed by the Company or a member of the Controlled Group, nor affects the company’s right to terminate employment with or without cause. No benefit under the Plan is subject to anticipation, alienation, sale, transfer, assignment, pledge, encumbrance, charge, execution, attachment, garnishment, or any other legal process; any such attempt is void and allows the Administrator to forfeit all further rights to the benefit. Additionally, a participant’s account may be reduced by the amount of any tax obligation paid by the Company or a member of the Controlled Group on behalf of a participant, beneficiary, or other person if such individual fails to reimburse the Company. No funds are segregated or earmarked for or in the account of any participant.
